idiom_name: discriminated union of interfaces with named child fields + never-based exhaustiveness
implementation_notes: The accepted modelling of an irregular AST in TypeScript is one interface per node kind carrying that kind's named children plus a literal discriminant (interface Binary { kind: "binary"; left: Expr; op: string; right: Expr }) unioned into type Expr = Literal | Binary; switch (e.kind) narrows the union so each arm sees exactly its own fields, and an assertNever arm documents exhaustiveness - the handbook's own discriminated-union example shows why an optional-property encoding fails to narrow. Class hierarchies remain common where a library ships runtime node objects (the TypeScript compiler's own AST), but the union form is the type-level default.
pitfalls: Narrowing only works through a literal discriminant: with optional-property shapes the compiler cannot relate fields to the tag (the handbook's counter-example), and strictNullChecks alone does not fix that.
Exhaustiveness is a convention - the never assignment in the default arm - not a compiler guarantee; omit the arm and new node kinds pass through.
Structural typing lets unrelated node shapes unify silently, so a stray extra field can make two node types assignable to each other.
